profileName: Databiz — Second-Act Vision, Executive Presentations & Storycraft (B2 → C1)

watchOuts.tag: Executive Storycraft · Translating Big Ideas Into Concrete Moments
watchOuts.title: Anchor High-Level Philosophy in One Specific Scene Before Zooming Out
watchOuts.detail: Strategic thinkers naturally jump straight to big-picture principles ('freedom', 'legacy', 'value'). In presentations and conversations, hook your audience first with a single concrete moment—a specific boardroom decision, a flight between Santo Domingo and Toronto, or a quiet morning after closing your exit—before stating the broader lesson.

watchOuts.tag: Mandarin L1 Grammar · Past Tense & Articles Under Pressure
watchOuts.title: Locking In Past-Time Markers & Countable Noun Articles ('a / the')
watchOuts.detail: Because Mandarin expresses time with context rather than verb endings and has no articles, fast executive storytelling often drops '-ed' endings ('When we close the deal' → 'When we closed the deal') or omits 'a / the' before singular nouns ('We built data platform' → 'We built a data platform').

watchOuts.tag: Mandarin L1 Pronunciation · Consonant Clusters, /r/ vs /l/, and /v/ vs /w/
watchOuts.title: Releasing Final Consonant Clusters Without Dropping Endings
watchOuts.detail: Keep final consonants audible in high-frequency business words ('growth', 'result', 'world', 'exit', 'market'), distinguish curled/bunched /r/ from tongue-tip /l/ ('role' vs. 'low', 'risk' vs. 'list'), and touch upper teeth to lower lip on /v/ ('value', 'venture', 'invest') instead of rounding like /w/.

watchOuts.tag: B2 → C1 Business Lexicon · Upgrading Repetition
watchOuts.title: Replacing Generic Words ('good', 'big', 'do', 'make value') With Executive Verbs
watchOuts.detail: Your ideas are already C1-level; upgrade recurring B2 verbs so your vocabulary matches your strategic depth. Swap 'make a big business' for 'scale a multi-million-dollar enterprise', 'after selling' for 'post-exit', and 'useful second life' for 'a purposeful second act'.

watchOuts.tag: Presentation Pacing · Word-Stress Rhythm Over Syllable-by-Syllable Delivery
watchOuts.title: Punching Key Meaning Words and Pausing Between Thought Groups
watchOuts.detail: Mandarin gives every syllable equal weight, which can make English presentations sound dense when delivering complex cross-border strategy. Slow down slightly, stress the single most important word in each clause, and pause a full beat after key takeaways.

scenarios.title: Keynote Storycraft: 'What Makes the Second Half of Life Truly Valuable After Financial Success?'
scenarios.prompt: Deliver a 2-minute opening talk to a peer group of middle-aged founders and executives. Share what exiting a multi-million-dollar company taught you about identity, money, and purpose—moving from one vivid personal scene into your core philosophy for building a meaningful second act.

scenarios.title: Cross-Border Pitch: Connecting Opportunities Across the Dominican Republic, USA, and Canada
scenarios.prompt: Present your cross-border business thesis to potential North American or Caribbean partners. Clearly explain why your experience scaling in China gives you a unique edge in spotting opportunities across the US, Canada, and the Dominican Republic—using crisp past-to-present tense transitions.

scenarios.title: Pocket Story - Catalyst: Building and Closing a Multi-Million-Dollar Exit
scenarios.prompt: Tell the story of the turning point that defined your original business—not as a dry timeline, but as a high-stakes decision where you saw something others missed, took a calculated risk, and saw it through to a successful close.

scenarios.title: Pocket Story - External Passion: What Soccer Teaches About Vision, Timing, and Reinvention
scenarios.prompt: Use soccer as a living metaphor for business and middle-aged reinvention—comparing a young striker's nonstop sprint to a veteran midfielder who reads the whole pitch, conserves energy, and delivers the decisive pass.

scenarios.title: Executive Roundtable: Giving Candid Advice to a Younger Founder Burning Out
scenarios.prompt: A 32-year-old founder asks whether grinding 80 hours a week is the only path to a big exit. Respond with warmth, authority, and concrete storytelling—balancing hard-won business realism with your perspective on long-term value.

customCards.term: B2 → C1 Executive Upgrade (Second-Act Purpose): Upgrade "After I sold my company, I started thinking about how middle-aged men can make their remaining life more useful."
customCards.definition: "After closing my exit, I began asking a deeper question: how do men in midlife design a second act defined by real contribution rather than just accumulation?"
customCards.example: Phrases like 'closing my exit', 'design a second act', and 'contribution rather than accumulation' give philosophical ideas C1 executive weight.
customCards.note: Storycraft & Lexicon: Elevate reflective themes with crisp, memorable contrast.

customCards.term: Grammar Polish (Past Tense & Articles): Correct the missing markers: "In 2019, we launch new data product and sign major client in North America."
customCards.definition: "In 2019, we launched a new data product and signed a major client in North America."
customCards.example: Anchor completed past milestones with '-ed' ('launched', 'signed') and place 'a' before singular countable nouns ('a new product', 'a major client').
customCards.note: Grammar Accuracy: Clean past-tense endings keep founder track-record stories sharp and credible.

customCards.term: Pronunciation Drill (/v/ vs /w/ & Final Clusters): Read aloud clearly: "We evaluate every venture across five world markets before investing."
customCards.definition: Touch upper teeth gently to lower lip on 'evaluate / every / venture / five / investing' (/v/), and release the final '-ld' and '-ts' in 'world markets'.
customCards.example: Keep 'value' and 'venture' distinct from 'w'-initial words like 'world' and 'we'.
customCards.note: Mandarin L1 Clarity: Strong /v/ contact and crisp word endings boost instant clarity in international meetings.

customCards.term: Presentation Hook (Zoom In Before Zooming Out): Upgrade this abstract slide opener: "Today I want to talk about cross-border opportunity between China, the US, Canada, and the Dominican Republic."
customCards.definition: "Six months ago, sitting across from a supplier in Santo Domingo, I noticed the exact same supply-chain bottleneck I solved in China ten years earlier."
customCards.example: Start with a time, a place, and an observation—then zoom out to your regional thesis.
customCards.note: Executive Storycraft: Concrete opening scenes lock audience attention in the first 15 seconds.

customCards.term: Soccer Analogy for Midlife Leadership: Frame the shift from youthful hustle to veteran strategy in two punchy sentences.
customCards.definition: "In your twenties, you play like a winger—chasing every ball at full sprint. In your forties and fifties, you play central midfield—reading the space early and making the pass that changes the game."
customCards.example: Sports analogies translate complex leadership shifts effortlessly across US, Canadian, and Latin American business cultures.
customCards.note: Metaphor & Persuasion: Vivid metaphors make your big-picture thinking immediately relatable.

customCards.term: Pronunciation Drill (/r/ vs /l/ & Word Stress): Read with strong stress on bold words: "Our **long-term** **role** is to **build** **lasting** **value** across the **region**."
customCards.definition: Touch tongue tip behind top teeth for 'long / role / build / lasting / value'; pull tongue back without touching for 'role' (/r/) and 'region' (/r/).
customCards.example: Punch the stressed content words and let small words ('is', 'to', 'the') stay light and fast.
customCards.note: Presentation Rhythm: Contrast between stressed and unstressed syllables makes presentations engaging and natural.
